paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much individual training examples help or hurt a model. A single score for an entire example can hide an important distinction: some of its cells may contain useful information while others are noisy. Calling the whole example harmful therefore does not explain which parts caused the problem.

2D-OOB addresses this by evaluating samples and their individual cells together. Its out-of-bag estimation framework identifies helpful or detrimental examples while also locating the cells responsible for those assessments. This makes the resulting values more interpretable because an example's overall contribution can be connected to particular pieces of its contents.

The experiments report leading performance across multiple applications and an exponential speed advantage. More specifically, the method shows promising results for finding and correcting unusual values at the cell level and locating backdoor triggers in poisoned data. These findings suggest that joint valuation can support targeted data repair, preserving useful parts of examples while identifying the parts that need attention.
neurips-2024-2d-oob-attributing-data-con.tldr: 2D-OOB jointly values training examples and their individual cells to identify which pieces of data help or harm a model.

paragraphs: Detecting objects in a three-dimensional point cloud requires understanding both local shapes and the wider scene. Transformer attention has worked well for this task, but its quadratic computational cost becomes difficult as point clouds become more detailed. This paper explores Mamba, a state space model with linear sequence complexity, for indoor object detection.

The proposed 3DET-Mamba divides the point cloud into patches. An Inner Mamba module captures geometry within those patches, while a Dual Mamba module handles scene-level information through spatial distribution and continuity. A third, Query-aware Mamba module uses learned queries to turn the resulting contextual features into a set of detected objects.

This design connects local geometric processing, global scene modeling, and object prediction within one detection system. In experiments on indoor detection benchmarks including ScanNet, the authors report improvements over 3DETR: AP25 rises from 65.0% to 70.4%, and AP50 from 47.0% to 54.4%. The findings support Mamba's usefulness beyond language modeling, specifically for extracting object information from indoor three-dimensional scenes.
neurips-2024-3det-mamba-causal-sequence-.tldr: 3DET-Mamba combines local, global, and query-guided state space modules to improve indoor 3D object detection.

paragraphs: Strong scores on a familiar mathematics benchmark may reflect both reasoning and exposure to similar questions during training. To investigate this possibility, the authors commission GSM1k, a new collection of grade-school mathematics problems designed to match the established GSM8k benchmark in style and difficulty.

The comparison controls for characteristics including human success rates, solution length in steps, and answer magnitude. Evaluating open- and closed-source language models reveals accuracy drops of up to 8% on GSM1k. Several model families show evidence of systematic overfitting across almost all tested model sizes, making the performance difference more than an isolated observation.

The authors also find a positive association between a model's likelihood of generating a GSM8k example and its performance gap across the two benchmarks. This suggests partial memorization in some models, rather than proving that memorization explains every gap. Many models, especially frontier models, show little evidence of overfitting. All evaluated models still broadly generalize to new problems absent from their training data, so the findings qualify benchmark success without dismissing mathematical generalization.
neurips-2024-a-careful-examination-of-la.tldr: A fresh benchmark matched to GSM8k reveals evidence of overfitting in some language models alongside broad generalization to new mathematics problems.

paragraphs: Camera and LiDAR models provide complementary information for autonomous driving. When their separately pretrained backbones are combined, however, the authors argue that some features become redundant across the two sensors. Pruning methods designed for a single input modality can struggle to identify this particular kind of duplication.

AlterMOMA tests the relationship between the backbones by alternately deactivating parameters in each modality. When information from one backbone disappears, previously redundant features in the other backbone become active again. Observing this reactivation helps identify features that overlap across modalities and the parameters associated with them.

The framework then uses AlterEva, an importance-scoring function based on changes in loss as modality parameters are activated and deactivated, to guide pruning. This matters because a parameter's contribution is assessed in relation to the other sensor's available information. Experiments on nuScene and KITTI span different tasks, baseline models, and pruning algorithms. The authors report that AlterMOMA outperforms existing pruning methods and achieves leading performance in these evaluations.
neurips-2024-altermoma-fusion-redundancy.tldr: AlterMOMA alternately masks camera and LiDAR components to expose cross-modal redundancy and guide parameter pruning.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves discrete choices, but neural solvers often learn by allowing those choices to take continuous values. This makes direct optimization possible without labeled solutions. It also creates two difficulties: learning can get stuck at local optima, and the final continuous answer must be converted back into discrete decisions.

Continuous Relaxation Annealing, or CRA, makes that conversion part of learning itself. It adds a penalty whose role changes over time. Early on, the penalty favors continuous solutions and smooths the non-convex objective. Later, it pushes the solution toward discreteness, removing the need for a separate artificial rounding procedure after learning.

The approach therefore coordinates exploration of the relaxed problem with production of a discrete answer. Experiments report substantial performance gains over existing unsupervised neural solvers and greedy algorithms on complex combinatorial problems. They also show faster learning and elimination of the separate rounding stage. These results support controlling the relaxation throughout optimization rather than treating the return to discrete choices as an independent final operation.
neurips-2024-controlling-continuous-rela.tldr: CRA gradually changes a training penalty from favoring continuous solutions to enforcing discrete ones, improving neural combinatorial optimization without post-training rounding.

paragraphs: Understanding a comic can require more than recognizing objects or describing what happens in each image. Humor may depend on how two panels contradict one another, especially when the narrative does not unfold in a straightforward sequence. This paper examines whether large vision language models can interpret that relationship.

The authors introduce YesBut, a benchmark centered on two-panel comics whose narratives create a humorous contradiction. Its tasks span different levels of difficulty, from understanding literal content to reasoning about the deeper narrative. This range allows evaluation to examine both what models recognize in the panels and how they interpret the connection between them.

Experiments with recent commercial and open-source models show that even leading systems struggle with these comics. The result identifies a challenge in interpreting human creative expression despite broad progress on other vision and language tasks. YesBut makes that challenge concrete: successful comprehension requires connecting the panels' meanings and explaining the contradictory narrative that carries the humor.
neurips-2024-cracking-the-code-of-juxtap.tldr: The YesBut benchmark finds that leading vision language models still struggle to understand humor created by contradictory two-panel narratives.

paragraphs: Editing a model requires identifying which internal components matter for particular predictions. DisCEdit approaches this through feature distributions, building on the hypothesis that trained convolutional models contain filters essential for distinguishing classes. It uses this perspective for both structured pruning and selectively reducing a model's ability to recognize one class.

The method defines discriminative ability through Bayes error, equivalently expressed using total variation distance between feature distributions. Because directly computing that distance is intractable, the authors derive lower bounds using witness functions. These bounds require no assumptions about the underlying distributions, extending approaches that assumed Gaussian feature distributions.

The bounds identify subnetworks associated with class-specific predictions. The resulting pruning algorithm requires neither training data nor the loss function. For selective forgetting on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, the authors report an average reduction of over 80% in a targeted class's accuracy with minimal impact on remaining classes. For ResNet50 on ImageNet, they report 40.8% sparsity with a 2.6% accuracy drop and minimal fine-tuning. These results demonstrate two uses of the same component-identification principle.
neurips-2024-discedit-model-editing-by-i.tldr: DisCEdit uses distribution-based measures of component importance to support structured pruning and selective class forgetting.

paragraphs: Increasing model size and training data has driven progress in language and vision, but this paper investigates how that relationship applies to molecular pretraining. The authors study whether molecular models exhibit systematic scaling behavior and whether larger pretrained models improve performance on downstream molecular tasks.

Their model uses a two-track transformer to integrate information about individual atoms, molecular graphs, and three-dimensional geometry. Alongside this architecture, they examine power-law relationships between validation loss and three resources: model size, dataset size, and computation. They scale the model to 1.1 billion parameters using pretraining data containing 800 million molecular conformations.

The experiments show consistent downstream improvement as model size increases. The largest model outperforms existing methods, with reported average improvements of 27% on QM9 and 14% on COMPAS-1D. These findings connect the scaling investigation to practical task performance. The contribution combines a molecular representation architecture with evidence that expanding training resources can produce useful gains in the evaluated molecular setting.
neurips-2024-exploring-molecular-pretrai.tldr: A molecular transformer integrating atomic, graph, and geometric information shows consistent downstream gains as it scales to 1.1 billion parameters.

paragraphs: Person re-identification models need representations that remain useful when deployment images differ from training images. Data augmentation can help, but the authors identify a polarized effect: certain augmentations improve performance within the training distribution while worsening performance outside it. They connect this behavior to sparse, less uniformly distributed representations.

Balancing Alignment and Uniformity, or BAU, addresses the geometry of that representation space. It applies alignment and uniformity losses to both original and augmented images. A weighting strategy evaluates the reliability of augmented samples and adjusts their contribution to alignment, so the framework can account for differences in augmentation quality.

BAU also encourages uniformity separately within each source domain, supporting the learning of features that carry across domains. Experiments report that this combination makes better use of augmentation and achieves leading performance without complicated training procedures. The significance is that augmentation's usefulness depends partly on how training organizes representations: preserving useful alignment while maintaining uniformity can improve generalization to unfamiliar image distributions.
neurips-2024-generalizable-person-re-ide.tldr: BAU balances representation alignment and uniformity to make image augmentation more effective for person re-identification across domains.

paragraphs: Sampling from a discrete distribution becomes difficult when probability is concentrated around many separate modes. Gradient information can guide a sampler toward likely configurations, but it can also keep the sampler near one local mode. The paper introduces automatic cyclical schedules to balance finding new modes with exploring those already reached.

The method changes step size cyclically: large steps encourage movement toward other modes, while small steps explore a mode more closely. A second schedule adjusts proposal balancing to suit those step sizes and maintain efficient Markov-chain behavior. An automatic tuning procedure sets the schedules' hyperparameters, reducing the manual adjustment needed across datasets.

These components work together because changing movement size also changes what makes a proposal effective. The authors prove finite-time convergence and inference guarantees for general discrete distributions, and their experiments report superior sampling performance on complex multimodal distributions. The findings support adapting both exploration scale and proposal balance over time, rather than relying on one fixed sampling behavior throughout the process.
neurips-2024-gradient-based-discrete-sam.tldr: Automatically tuned cyclical schedules help gradient-based discrete samplers alternate between discovering modes and exploring them efficiently.

paragraphs: A robot following a spoken or written grasp instruction needs to connect language with detailed hand-object interactions. The paper introduces Dexterous Grasp as You Say, a task focused on generating dexterous grasps that reflect human commands. A central obstacle is the shortage of grasp datasets paired with natural, fine-grained language guidance.

To address that obstacle, the authors create DexGYSNet, combining grasp annotations with flexible human language instructions. Their construction process uses hand-object interaction retargeting and language-model-assisted annotation to keep data creation cost-efficient. The dataset supplies the connection between detailed grasp configurations and the intentions expressed in language.

The accompanying DexGYSGrasp framework separates learning into two progressive objectives. Its first component learns a grasp distribution emphasizing intention alignment and diversity. Its second improves grasp quality while retaining consistency with the instruction. This separation makes the roles of intent, variety, and refinement explicit. The authors validate the approach through extensive experiments on DexGYSNet and in real-world environments, supporting its stated ability to generate varied, high-quality grasps aligned with language.
neurips-2024-grasp-as-you-say-language-g.tldr: DexGYSNet and DexGYSGrasp connect natural-language instructions to diverse dexterous grasps through intent-focused generation followed by quality refinement.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible description of coordinated behavior does not necessarily produce a useful multi-agent plan. This paper addresses that gap by putting a language-guided simulator inside a multi-agent reinforcement learning pipeline. The aim is to give generated answers a basis in learned interactions and task rewards.

The simulator separates how the world changes from how outcomes are valued. Its dynamics component combines an image tokenizer with a causal transformer to generate successive interaction transitions. Its reward component uses a bidirectional transformer trained under language guidance by maximizing the likelihood of expert demonstration trajectories.

Given a current-state image and a task description, the framework trains a joint policy inside this learned world. It then runs the converged policy through the dynamics model and returns the resulting image sequence as its answer. Experiments on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge report stronger performance on both training and unseen tasks. The framework also produces consistent interaction sequences and explainable rewards at interaction states, connecting its proposed actions with learned consequences and evaluations.
neurips-2024-grounded-answers-for-multi-.tldr: A language-guided world model trains coordinated policies and generates visual answers grounded in simulated interactions and learned rewards.

paragraphs: Optimization theory often explains why training should converge by assuming that the loss function has a convenient mathematical structure. For deep networks, establishing those assumptions can be difficult. The Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality is a prominent example: validating it can demand levels of over-parameterization that are impractical for the models being studied.

The authors propose a new class of functions intended to describe deep-learning loss landscapes without requiring such extensive over-parameterization. Their condition also allows saddle points. This matters because the theoretical description can accommodate landscape structure that a more restrictive assumption would rule out.

Under the proposed assumption, the paper proves convergence guarantees for gradient-based optimizers. The authors then support the assumption through theoretical analysis and experiments across diverse deep-learning models. The guarantees remain conditional on that landscape assumption; the contribution is a different mathematical basis for analyzing training. Together, the analysis and experiments aim to narrow the gap between structures convenient for optimization proofs and structures observed in practical neural networks.
neurips-2024-loss-landscape-characteriza.tldr: A new loss-landscape assumption permits saddle points and yields conditional convergence guarantees without requiring extensive network over-parameterization.

paragraphs: Some fast attention methods replace or approximate softmax with functions that produce low-rank matrices when applied entry by entry to query-key scores. Low-degree polynomials have this useful property. The paper asks whether other functions can provide the same structural route to faster attention.

Using a new tool based on group representation theory, the authors prove that low-degree polynomials are the only piecewise continuous functions with the specified low-rank property. This suggests that attention acceleration through this particular low-rank mechanism depends on functions that can be approximated by polynomials. The result characterizes the available functions rather than introducing a new attention benchmark.

The same mathematical tool also yields complete classifications of positive definite kernels based on Manhattan distance and functions that transform Manhattan distances into Manhattan distances. These extend foundational classifications concerning Euclidean distance. Additional results address functions that preserve stable rank and may be useful in algorithm design. The unifying contribution, called representation theory of the hyperrectangle, connects questions about attention matrices, kernel construction, and transformations of distance.
neurips-2024-metric-transforms-and-low-r.tldr: A representation-theoretic tool characterizes functions enabling a particular low-rank attention mechanism and classifies Manhattan-distance kernels and transforms.

paragraphs: What happens when successive models train on data generated by earlier versions of themselves? This paper studies the resulting performance degradation, known as model collapse, in regression with Gaussian data. It analyzes both low- and high-dimensional asymptotic settings, covering under-parameterized and over-parameterized regimes.

The authors derive formulas describing how test error grows across model generations and how that growth depends on covariance structure, regularization, label noise, and dataset size. They separate the effects on bias and variance. Their analysis includes linear growth with iteration count and also shows that exponentially fast collapse can occur in an over-parameterized setting even without noise.

Under the special conditions of polynomially decaying spectral and source behavior, the paper derives modified scaling laws with transitions from faster to slower rates. It also proposes adaptive regularization as a way to mitigate collapse. Experiments validate the theoretical results. The contribution is a quantitative account within a specified regression setting, showing how recursive synthetic-data training interacts with model size and other problem parameters.
neurips-2024-model-collapse-demystified-.tldr: An analysis of Gaussian regression quantifies recursive synthetic-data degradation and proposes adaptive regularization to mitigate it.

paragraphs: Customizing foundation models with small task-specific adapters reduces training costs, but those adapters still need to be stored and run at the model server. Prompt tuning offers another route by placing task-specific information in input prefixes. Its drawback is that traditional approaches perform worse than alternatives such as LoRA.

Low-Rank Prompt Adaptation, or LoPA, aims to close that performance gap while retaining prompt-based customization. It generates soft prompts that combine information shared across a task with information tailored to each individual instance. A low-rank decomposition of the instance-specific prompt component keeps the number of parameters small.

The authors evaluate LoPA across natural-language understanding and code generation and understanding tasks, using foundation models of different sizes. They report performance comparable to leading parameter-efficient methods and full fine-tuning, with greater parameter efficiency and no need for a server-based adapter. The approach matters because it connects effective customization to the input interface while explicitly balancing reusable task knowledge with adaptation to the current example.
neurips-2024-prompt-tuning-strikes-back-.tldr: LoPA uses low-rank, instance-adapted soft prompts to achieve competitive model customization without server-based adapters.

paragraphs: Visual grounding locates the object in an image described by a natural-language expression. DETR-based approaches predict object coordinates directly, but their decoder queries often begin with random values or linguistic embeddings that lack target-related context. Existing query learning also relies on the deepest image features, overlooking other feature levels.

RefFormer addresses these issues with a query adaptation module integrated into CLIP and a decoder designed for the grounding task. The module generates a referential query that supplies relevant context at the start of decoding. This gives the decoder information to guide its attention toward the referred object and reduces the difficulty of learning that focus.

The query module also serves as an adapter, allowing the method to retain CLIP's learned knowledge without updating the backbone's parameters. Experiments report effectiveness and efficiency, with performance exceeding leading approaches on five grounding benchmarks. The central contribution is to improve the information used to initiate object localization, alongside the decoder that turns that information into a prediction.
neurips-2024-referencing-where-to-focus-.tldr: RefFormer supplies target-related referential queries to a grounding decoder, improving object localization while keeping the CLIP backbone frozen.

paragraphs: Time-series models often encounter a shift between training and deployment data. Domain adaptation can address that shift, but effective models may be too complex for resource-limited monitoring devices. Knowledge distillation transfers information from a teacher to a smaller student, yet simply matching outputs across all available samples can ignore the student's limited capacity.

Reinforced Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation, or RCD-KD, makes target-domain sample selection adaptive. A reinforcement-learning module uses a reward function to learn which target samples are suitable for transferring knowledge to the current student. This connects the selection policy to what the student's network can handle.

The framework also includes a domain discriminator to support transfer of knowledge that remains useful across domains. Its two mechanisms therefore address both the capacity gap and the distribution shift. Experiments and analyses on four public time-series datasets report better results than other leading methods. The findings support selecting transfer examples dynamically instead of treating every target example as equally suitable for a smaller model.
neurips-2024-reinforced-cross-domain-kno.tldr: RCD-KD uses reinforcement learning to select target-domain examples suited to a student's capacity while transferring domain-invariant knowledge.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimization methods are popular because they reduce the effort needed to tune learning rates. This paper introduces KATE, an adaptation of AdaGrad designed around scale invariance. It examines the algorithm through both mathematical guarantees and numerical comparisons with established adaptive optimizers.

The authors prove KATE's scale invariance for generalized linear models. Separately, for general smooth non-convex optimization problems, they establish a convergence rate of O((log T)/sqrt(T)). This matches the best-known rates stated for AdaGrad and Adam. The scope of the two results differs: the scale-invariance proof concerns generalized linear models, while the convergence result applies to the broader smooth non-convex setting.

Experiments compare KATE with AdaGrad and Adam on several problems, including image and text classification using real data. KATE consistently outperforms AdaGrad and matches or exceeds Adam in all scenarios considered. These findings combine competitive theoretical convergence with favorable empirical performance, providing support for the proposed AdaGrad variant across the tested optimization and machine-learning tasks.
neurips-2024-remove-that-square-root-a-n.tldr: KATE adapts AdaGrad with proven scale invariance for generalized linear models and competitive convergence and empirical performance.

paragraphs: Molecular generators can search beyond the compounds available in fixed screening libraries, but their proposed molecules may be difficult to synthesize. That creates a practical obstacle to experimental validation. Reaction-GFlowNet, or RGFN, addresses this by making chemical reactions the space in which generation operates.

RGFN extends the GFlowNet framework to construct candidates using a proposed collection of reactions and building blocks. The authors report that this provides synthesizability directly within generation while maintaining comparable candidate quality. With their chosen reactions and building blocks, the accessible molecular space is orders of magnitude larger than existing screening libraries and is coupled with low synthesis cost.

The approach also scales to very large fragment libraries, further expanding the possible compounds. Evaluations use several kinds of oracle models, including pretrained proxies and GPU-accelerated docking, to demonstrate effectiveness. The significance is the connection between search breadth and construction feasibility: the model explores a large space through reaction-based choices, so synthesis considerations are built into how candidates are produced.
neurips-2024-rgfn-synthesizable-molecula.tldr: RGFN generates molecules through chemical reactions, combining a large search space with synthesis-aware candidate construction.

paragraphs: Models that predict dynamical systems repeatedly into the future can accumulate errors at each step. Those errors make long rollouts increasingly unreliable. This paper addresses the problem by allowing encoded physical fields to exchange information, so predictions can account for relationships between the system's state variables.

State-Exchange Attention, or SEA, uses multi-head cross-attention for multidirectional communication across fields. Every state variable can exchange information with the others, helping the model capture physical relationships and symmetries. The authors also introduce an efficient mesh autoencoder, similar in style to a vision transformer, that creates spatially coherent embeddings for many mesh cells.

The SEA-integrated transformer reports leading rollout-error performance, reducing error by 88% and 91% relative to the two named comparison systems. The SEA module alone can reduce error by 97% for state variables strongly dependent on other system states. These results highlight the usefulness of cross-field information, particularly when predicting one quantity depends heavily on understanding the behavior of other quantities.
neurips-2024-sea-state-exchange-attentio.tldr: SEA enables information exchange among physical fields and substantially reduces reported errors in dynamical-system rollouts.

paragraphs: A strong pretrained student can sometimes learn more than a weaker teacher explicitly provides. It may correct the teacher's incorrect predictions and generalize to examples where the teacher is uncertain, even when those examples are excluded from training. The paper calls these effects pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion.

The authors argue that existing weak-supervision theory does not account for both effects. They introduce a bound based on expansion properties of the data distribution and the student's hypothesis class. The underlying intuition is that copying the teacher's mistakes may be difficult for the student without also making additional errors elsewhere.

This provides a conditional explanation for how incomplete or incorrect supervision can still support stronger performance. The bound extends results from co-training and self-training, bringing error correction and expanded coverage into one analysis. The authors also show that the relevant expansion properties can be checked using finite data and provide empirical evidence that they hold in practice. The contribution connects observed weak-to-strong behavior with structural properties that can be investigated rather than merely assumed.
neurips-2024-theoretical-analysis-of-wea.tldr: A new theoretical bound explains how strong students can correct weak teachers and generalize beyond their confident predictions under expansion conditions.

paragraphs: WildTeaming studies jailbreak tactics found in naturally occurring user-chatbot conversations. It discovers 5.7 thousand distinct tactic clusters and combines selected tactics to explore further adversarial prompts. The authors report that this process uncovers previously unidentified vulnerabilities in frontier language models and produces more diverse, successful attacks than leading comparison methods.

The framework also creates WildJailbreak, an open synthetic safety-training dataset containing 262 thousand prompt-response pairs. It includes both direct and adversarial requests. Crucially, the data pairs harmful queries with benign queries that look similar in form but lack harmful intent, helping training distinguish danger from merely suspicious wording.

The authors use extensive training and evaluation to study how data scale and composition interact with model capabilities. They identify training properties associated with appropriate safeguards, reduced over-refusal, effective handling of direct and adversarial requests, and little or no decline in general capabilities. All dataset components contribute to that balance. The contribution links realistic adversarial discovery with training resources designed to improve safety while preserving responses to legitimate requests.
neurips-2024-wildteaming-at-scale-from-i.tldr: WildTeaming turns naturally occurring jailbreak tactics into adversarial tests and a large safety dataset designed to improve safeguards without excessive refusal.

paragraphs: A language model's tokenizer determines how text is split into vocabulary items. A tokenizer suited to English can produce inefficiently long sequences for other languages or code, even when the model can handle those tasks. Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer asks how to replace that tokenizer without first retraining the model for the replacement.

The main challenge is assigning useful embeddings to the new vocabulary. The authors train a hypernetwork that takes a tokenizer as input and predicts its embeddings. Experiments show that this network generalizes to unfamiliar tokenizers for both encoder and decoder models, including XLM-R and Mistral-7B.

The transferred models approach their original performance on cross-lingual and coding tasks while substantially shortening token sequences. The remaining performance gap can be closed quickly through continued training on fewer than one billion tokens, so the initial zero-shot result is close rather than identical. A hypernetwork trained for a base model also transfers to its fine-tuned variants without extra training, supporting more flexible reuse of tokenizer adaptation.
neurips-2024-zero-shot-tokenizer-transfe.tldr: A hypernetwork predicts embeddings for new tokenizers, enabling near-original model performance with shorter sequences before additional adaptation training.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination asks an agent to cooperate with partners it did not encounter during training. Evaluation is difficult because the partners selected for testing may differ from those encountered during deployment. A score against an unrepresentative partner population can therefore give an incomplete picture of the agent's ability to generalize.

ZSC-Eval addresses both partner selection and measurement. It first generates candidate partners using rewards that favor different behaviors, aiming to approximate the deployment partner distribution. It then selects evaluation partners using Best-Response Diversity and measures generalization across them with a metric called Best-Response Proximity.

The authors use the toolkit to benchmark coordination algorithms in Overcooked and Google Research Football. They also conduct a human experiment to verify consistency between the toolkit and human evaluation. The contribution is an evaluation process that explicitly considers whom an agent must cooperate with, rather than reducing assessment to performance against a single convenient partner set. It supplies a shared benchmark and metrics for studying generalization across unfamiliar collaborators.
neurips-2024-zsc-eval-an-evaluation-tool.tldr: ZSC-Eval evaluates cooperation with unseen partners through behavior-based partner generation, diversity-based selection, and a dedicated generalization metric.
